The Africa Guide: Camp Selection, Safari Seasons, and Six Regions That Don't Overlap

Why the camp you choose matters more than the country. Six African regions — from the Okavango Delta to gorilla country to Morocco's medinas — and what makes each one the right choice for a specific trip.

Home › Travel Journal › Destination Guide › Africa
MS
Mark Sole Founder & Travel Director, Hit Your Mark Travel
Share

No destination in the world is planned worse than Africa. This is a continent of 54 countries and more distinct ecosystems than any other landmass on earth — and most people approach it as if it were a single product called "safari" with a few options to select from a dropdown menu. Country. Season. Budget. Click. The result is a significant number of trips that don't deliver what was imagined, not because Africa failed but because the wrong version of it was booked for the wrong reasons.

The single most consequential decision in planning an African safari is not the country, not the season, and not the budget tier. It is the camp. More specifically, it is the guide. A talented, deeply experienced guide at a mid-tier camp in a good ecosystem will produce a better safari experience than a disengaged guide at the most expensive camp on the continent. The guide is the person who reads the sand at 5 a.m. and knows that a leopard passed here less than an hour ago. The guide is the one who stops the vehicle and says nothing for forty minutes while a pride of lions makes a kill, because they understand that narration is the wrong choice. The guide is the difference between watching wildlife and understanding it — and that difference is the difference between a good trip and one you'll spend the rest of your life trying to replicate.

This guide covers six African regions that each represent a fundamentally different travel experience. Two of them — Morocco and the Indian Ocean islands — have nothing to do with game drives. The remaining four each deliver a distinct version of the safari experience that doesn't substitute for the others. The goal is to give you the framework to select the right region, the right season, and the right camp before the first conversation with a travel advisor begins.

The Camp Selection Question

The best camps in Africa share a small number of qualities that are easy to ask about and surprisingly often not asked. The first is guide tenure — specifically, how long the current senior guides have been at that camp, in that specific ecosystem. An experienced guide who has spent eight years tracking animals in the Okavango Delta knows those waterways in a way that a newer guide does not, regardless of their general competence. The second is vehicle policy: how many vehicles go out at a time, and how many vehicles are permitted at a single sighting? Camps that limit vehicles per sighting deliver a fundamentally quieter, more immersive encounter with wildlife. The third is camp size. The best camps are small — typically six to twelve tents. The intimacy of a small camp changes the quality of every meal, every sundowner, every morning debrief.

A large camp with bus transfers to game drives is not a safari in the same category as a small camp with dedicated vehicles and guides who have been in that ecosystem for years. Both can be marketed identically. Both can look similar in photographs. The experience on the ground is not the same.

"In Africa, more than anywhere else on earth, the quality of your experience comes down to one person: your guide. The right guide at an average camp outperforms the wrong guide at an exceptional one."

Six Regions at a Glance

Below is a breakdown of each region — its character, the ecosystem, who it's right for, when to go, and the specific camps and properties worth knowing. A timing guide and property reference section follow.

The Regions
Six Regions. Six Different Africas.
01
East Africa — Kenya & Tanzania
The Migration First Safari Classic Africa
Masai Mara · Serengeti · Ngorongoro · Amboseli · Zanzibar
The most visited safari region in the world, and the one that defines most people's mental image of Africa — open savanna, acacia trees, vast horizons, and the wildebeest migration that moves between the Serengeti and Kenya's Masai Mara in a cycle that has continued for millennia. The river crossings at the Mara River between July and October, when hundreds of thousands of wildebeest push through crocodile-filled water in waves that last seconds and cost some of them their lives, are among the most visceral wildlife experiences on the planet.

Tanzania's Ngorongoro Crater is the most concentrated wildlife ecosystem in Africa — a collapsed volcanic caldera that functions as a natural enclosure for a permanent resident population of lions, elephants, black rhino, and flamingo-filled soda lakes. The Serengeti's southern plains produce the calving season between January and February, when approximately 400,000 wildebeest calves are born over a three-week period — a spectacle that draws fewer tourists than the river crossings but is, by most guides' assessment, the more extraordinary event. The standard itinerary adds Zanzibar at the end: dhow sailing, stone town architecture, and the Indian Ocean after the dust of the game drives.
Migration Crossings: July – October (Mara River) Calving Season: January – February (Southern Serengeti) Gateway: NBO (Nairobi) or JRO (Kilimanjaro) + bush flight Key Properties: Singita Grumeti (Serengeti), &Beyond Ngorongoro Crater Lodge, Mahali Mzuri (Mara)
02
Southern Africa — Botswana & Zimbabwe
Top Pick Repeat Safari Wilderness
Okavango Delta · Moremi · Chobe · Hwange · Mana Pools · Victoria Falls
The most sophisticated safari destination in Africa for the traveler who has been to East Africa and wants the next level. Botswana's high-value, low-volume policy — deliberately limiting tourism to protect the ecosystem — means that the camps here operate in concessions that no vehicle from another property can enter. You will not share a sighting. The Okavango Delta, a river that flows inland and fans out into a labyrinth of papyrus channels, floodplains, and permanent islands in the Kalahari Desert, is a wildlife ecosystem unlike any other on the continent. Water levels determine access and change the landscape seasonally in ways that make the experience genuinely different depending on the month.

Zimbabwe's Mana Pools, on the Zambezi floodplain, is the continent's most important destination for walking safari — experienced guides lead guests on foot through terrain where elephant, buffalo, and lion operate without barriers. The intimacy is absolute, and it is not appropriate for first-time safari travelers. Victoria Falls — the largest curtain of falling water on earth — anchors most Southern Africa itineraries as a single-night or two-night add-on, and earns its reputation without qualification.
Best Months: May – October (dry season concentrates wildlife at water) Okavango Peak Water: June – August (high flood, mokoro poling) Gateway: JNB (Johannesburg) + bush flight to Maun (Botswana) or VFA (Victoria Falls) Key Properties: Mombo Camp (Okavango), Zarafa Camp (Linyanti), Ruckomechi (Mana Pools)
03
South Africa
City + Bush Winelands Malaria-Free
Sabi Sand · Cape Town · Franschhoek · Garden Route · KwaZulu-Natal
The most accessible Africa destination for first-time visitors — direct flight infrastructure, English spoken throughout, no malaria in the main private reserve areas, and a Cape Town that competes with any city in the world for food, wine, and sheer visual drama. Table Mountain alone justifies the flight. The Cape Winelands — Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, Hemel-en-Aarde — produce Chenin Blanc and Pinotage in a setting that looks like a softer, greener version of Provence, and the restaurants at the top estates compete with anything in Western Europe.

The Sabi Sand Private Game Reserve, adjacent to Kruger National Park, is the finest malaria-free safari destination in Africa for travelers who aren't ready for the remote fly-in camps of Botswana. Londolozi — three tented camps on the Sand River — has been guiding safaris here since 1926 and has built a guide and tracker culture that sets the standard for the industry. The leopard density in the Sabi Sand is among the highest in the world, and the big-five sightings are genuinely exceptional. The classic South Africa itinerary: Cape Town and Winelands for four to five days, Sabi Sand for three to four nights, done.
Cape Town: October – April (summer); avoid June–July (cold and rainy) Sabi Sand: Year-round; May–September best for game viewing Gateway: CPT (Cape Town) or JNB (Johannesburg) direct from JFK, IAD, IAH Key Properties: Londolozi Tree Camp (Sabi Sand), Ellerman House (Cape Town), La Residence (Franschhoek)
04
Rwanda & the Great Apes
Gorilla Trekking Once-in-a-Life Small Groups
Volcanoes National Park · Nyungwe Forest · Congo Basin
The most genuinely different safari experience in Africa — nothing about it resembles a game drive. Gorilla trekking in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park begins before dawn, involves two to eight hours of hiking through dense forest at altitude, and ends when the habituated gorilla family is located. The hour-long visit — the maximum permitted time with any family — is conducted in near-silence, with guides managing the distance and behavior. A silverback that chooses to walk directly toward you, evaluate you, and continue past will reset whatever frame of reference you arrived with. Permits are USD $1,500 per person per visit and are limited to eight people per group per day.

Rwanda itself is one of the most striking African countries to visit — Kigali is the cleanest and most efficiently run capital city on the continent, with a food and coffee culture that surprises virtually every visitor. The genocide memorial is a necessary and carefully managed visit. The country's conservation record — mountain gorilla populations have grown from approximately 620 individuals in 2008 to over 1,000 today, due largely to Rwanda's protection framework — is among the most compelling conservation success stories on earth. Chimpanzee trekking in Nyungwe Forest adds a second primate experience to an itinerary that most travelers only allocate three days to, which is not enough.
Best Months: June – September and December – February (drier trekking) Gorilla Permits: USD $1,500 per person — book 3–6 months in advance Gateway: KGL (Kigali) — Ethiopian Airlines and RwandAir from major hubs Key Properties: Bisate Lodge (Volcanoes NP), Singita Kwitonda (Volcanoes NP), One&Only Nyungwe House
05
Morocco
Medina + Desert Culture No Game Drive
Marrakech · Fès · Atlas Mountains · Sahara · Essaouira
Africa's most visited destination, and the most distinct from every other region in this guide — a country with its own food culture, architectural tradition, souq economy, and Saharan landscape that shares geography with the continent but almost nothing else. Marrakech's medina is a genuinely disorienting place to arrive in: the souqs in the old city operate on medieval spatial logic, the riad hotels hidden behind unmarked wooden doors are among the most beautiful interior spaces in the world, and the cooking — preserved lemon, saffron, harissa, argan oil — belongs to a culinary tradition that rewards study rather than casual sampling.

The standard Morocco itinerary under-delivers because it tries to cover too much in too little time. Marrakech for four days — long enough for the medina to make sense, long enough to eat well — with a night at Aït-Ben-Haddou en route to the Sahara is a coherent trip. Fès deserves its own visit; the ancient medina of Fès el-Bali, UNESCO-listed and largely unchanged since the 14th century, is the most complete medieval city surviving in the Arab world. The Atlas Mountains in spring, when the High Atlas passes are clear and the valleys below are green, make for a drive that neither photographs accurately nor requires much planning to execute.
Best Months: March – May and September – November Avoid: July – August in Marrakech (extreme heat, 40°C+) Gateway: RAK (Marrakech) or CMN (Casablanca) — Royal Air Maroc direct from JFK Key Properties: La Mamounia (Marrakech), Amanjena (Marrakech), Dar Ahlam (Skoura)
06
Indian Ocean Islands
Seychelles Mozambique Post-Safari
Seychelles · Mozambique · Zanzibar · Madagascar · Mauritius
The Indian Ocean islands off Africa's east coast are the most extraordinary beach destinations on earth — and they are dramatically undervisited compared to the Caribbean or Southeast Asia beach circuits. The Seychelles Inner Islands sit on a granite shelf in the middle of the Indian Ocean; the rock formations at Anse Source d'Argent on La Digue are among the most distinctive coastal landscapes anywhere, and the outer atolls like Alphonse are so remote that the flight in — a light aircraft from Mahé over a hundred miles of open ocean — delivers the isolation before the boat has even left the dock.

Mozambique's Bazaruto Archipelago and Pemba in the north are what the Maldives looked like before the Maldives became famous — pristine reef systems, dugong in the seagrass, and a level of privacy that the most expensive Maldivian water villas can't replicate. Zanzibar, already mentioned in the East Africa context, functions as both a standalone destination and the natural beach appendix to a Tanzania safari. Madagascar is the most biologically extraordinary island in the world — 90% of its species found nowhere else — and is genuinely for the adventurous traveler rather than the resort guest.
Seychelles Best: April – May and October – November (shoulder; April/May have the calmest water) Mozambique Best: May – October (dry season; whale sharks July–August) Gateway: MRU (Mauritius) or NBO (Nairobi) connection to Seychelles; JNB to Mozambique Key Properties: North Island (Seychelles), &Beyond Benguerra Island (Mozambique), Fregate Island Private (Seychelles)
Timing
When to Go — by Season and by Ecosystem
Jun – Oct
Dry Season Peak
The primary safari window across sub-Saharan Africa. Vegetation thins, animals concentrate at permanent water sources, and game viewing reaches its maximum. Migration river crossings in the Mara peak July–October. Botswana's camps reach full flood in July–August. Book 10–12 months in advance for top camps.
Peak Safari
Jan – Feb
Calving Season
The most underbooked window in East Africa. Wildebeest calving in the Southern Serengeti — roughly 400,000 calves born over three weeks — draws predators in extraordinary concentrations. Fewer tourists than the migration crossing season, lower rates at most camps, and wildlife encounters that senior guides routinely rank as the best on the continent.
Best Value
Nov – Dec
Short Rains / Green
The short rains arrive in East Africa in November and generally clear by December. The landscape turns green, migratory birds return, and baby animals appear throughout. Photography improves with dramatic cloud formations and richer light. Some camps close in November — confirm operational status when booking. Lowest rates of the year.
Mar – May
Long Rains / Low
The long rainy season in East Africa. Many small camps close entirely. The Masai Mara and parts of the Serengeti become difficult to access. Botswana and Zimbabwe camps remain largely operational. Morocco is at its best — spring temperatures, wildflowers in the Atlas, comfortable Sahara nights. The right choice for the traveler who is flexible and values solitude.
Properties Worth Knowing
Eight Properties That Earn Their Rates
Not a comprehensive list — these are the specific camps and properties across Africa that consistently deliver what they promise, from the Okavango Delta to gorilla country to the Seychelles outer atolls.
Mombo Camp
Delta Icon
Chief's Island · Okavango Delta · Botswana
Consistently ranked as one of the finest safari camps on earth — eight tents on Chief's Island in the private concession of the same name, in an area of the Okavango that Wilderness Safaris has managed and protected for decades. The guide and tracker teams are among the most experienced in Botswana. The wildlife density on Chief's Island is exceptional year-round. The camp itself is intimate, beautifully designed, and fully all-inclusive. Book 12 months in advance for any desirable date in peak season.
Singita Grumeti
Migration Camp
Western Serengeti · Tanzania
A private 350,000-acre concession in the western Serengeti corridor — the route the migration follows between Tanzania and Kenya. Singita operates three properties within the concession (Sabora, Faru Faru, Sasakwa), each with a distinct character. The private concession means no other vehicles, ever. The guides have been working this terrain long enough to read the migration's trajectory weeks in advance. The wine cellar at Sasakwa is inexplicably excellent for a remote African camp.
Bisate Lodge
Gorilla Exclusive
Volcanoes National Park · Rwanda
Six forest villas on the edge of an ancient eroded volcanic cone, five minutes from the park entrance. Wilderness Safaris built Bisate as a high-end gorilla trekking base with a conservation mandate — the lodge is actively reforesting native Hagenia woodland around the property. The villas face directly into the Virunga volcano range. Gorilla permits are facilitated through the lodge, and the pre-trek briefing by the guides is among the best-prepared in Rwanda.
Londolozi Tree Camp
Bush Classic
Sabi Sand · Greater Kruger · South Africa
The most intimate of Londolozi's four camps on the Sand River — six suites built into a riverine forest canopy, with decks over the river and a guide-tracker partnership that has been refined across generations of game rangers. The leopard tracking here is among the most skilled on the continent. The malaria-free status of the Sabi Sand makes Londolozi the correct recommendation for families with children, first-time safari travelers, and anyone for whom the remote fly-in camps of Botswana represent too significant a logistical step.
La Mamounia
Medina Classic
Marrakech · Morocco
The reference property for Marrakech luxury since 1923 — a 209-room palace hotel set in seven acres of gardens adjacent to the old medina walls. Winston Churchill painted here; the guest registry reads like a century of European and American celebrity. The gardens are the finest in the city. The hammam is among the most accomplished in Morocco. The hotel was extensively renovated in 2009 and again recently; the result is a property that preserves its history while delivering contemporary service. Book the riad suites for the most authentic Moroccan interior experience.
North Island
Private Island
North Island · Seychelles
Eleven villas on a 201-hectare private island in the Seychelles Inner Islands, each with direct beach access on a beach that exists solely for the guest staying in that villa. The island is a conservation project as much as a hotel — the North Island Foundation has been restoring the native ecosystem since 2003, reintroducing giant tortoises, eradicating invasive species, and replanting native vegetation. The Seychelles warbler, locally extinct on the island for decades, now breeds here again. The rate is significant; what it buys is complete privacy, exceptional food, and an island that improves with each visit.
Zarafa Camp
Private Concession
Selinda Reserve · Northern Botswana
Four tents on the edge of the Zibadianja Lagoon in the Selinda Reserve — a 320,000-acre private concession in northern Botswana between the Okavango and the Linyanti. Great Plains Conservation operates the camp with one of the most experienced guide teams in the country. The lagoon attracts massive elephant herds in the dry season. The privacy is absolute. The dhow sunset cruise on the lagoon is among the most beautiful safari activities in Africa, which is a high bar to clear.
Ellerman House
Cape Town Estate
Bantry Bay · Cape Town · South Africa
Thirteen rooms and two villas in a restored Edwardian mansion on the Atlantic Seaboard, with a wine gallery of some 7,000 bottles and a collection of South African art throughout the property. The view from the pool terrace over the Atlantic — Lion's Head to the right, Robben Island in the middle distance — is the finest city vista in South Africa. The staff ratio is high enough that guests are known by name before arrival. The correct base for Cape Town before or after the Sabi Sand, a fifteen-minute drive from the Winelands and direct access to Camps Bay below.
